candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 28 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 29 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 30 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 31 not required. 32
candidates.context: ADHD is a common neurobehavioral disorder with onset in childhood. It is characterized by a 22 pattern of developmentally inappropriate and maladaptive inattentiveness, impulsivity, and 23 hyperactivity, resulting in impairment in family, social, academic, and occupational functioning. 24 Stimulant drugs (e.g., methylphenidate, amphetamine) are the most commonly prescribed 25 medications for treatment of ADHD. 26 II. candidates.context: In general, central nervous system stimulant drugs demonstrate a strong concentration-response 44 relationship for efficacy and safety (Kimko et al. 2012; Li et al. 2017). Therefore, sponsors can 45 develop formulations using the same active moiety with the objective of creating drug product- 46 specific release features intended to affect the shape of the pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and the 47 onset or duration of effect. candidates.statement: Women of reproductive potential are sometimes prescribed treatment for ADHD. Therefore, 134 sponsors should consider inclusion of pregnant women in clinical trials when scientifically and 135 ethically justified. If a sponsor excludes pregnant women from trial enrollment, the sponsor 136 should provide a scientific justification. 2 In addition, FDA may also require postmarketing safety 137 data collection pursuant to section 505(o)(3) of the FD&C Act. Sponsors should use existing 138 stimulant drug pregnancy registries (e.g., National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric 139 Medications) or establish their own registries . 140

candidates.statement: Methylphenidate and amphetamine drug products are available in multiple formulations with a 146 variety of dosage forms and durations of effect. The safety profiles of these products are well 147 characterized and their PD effects are tightly linked to their PK profiles. Thus, FDA believes it is 148 reasonable to rely on safety information from a listed drug to develop new methylphenidate or 149 amphetamine product via the 505(b)(2) application pathway and, in certain cases, it may be 150 reasonable to rely on the efficacy information. For instance, if a 505(b)(2) applicant can establish 151 a bridge to the relied-upon listed drug by demonstrating either bioequivalence or comparative 152 bioavailability of the proposed drug product with the listed drug, additional clinical trials may 153 not be necessary to support approval of the 505(b)(2) application. The sponsor should consult the 154 FDA’s drug product-specific guidances regarding trial design and data analysis for 155 bioequivalence evaluations. 3

candidates.statement: Unlike 505(b)(2) products, the safety, effectiveness, and PK-PD relationship for NMEs are 227 unknown and must be evaluated in the development program (i.e., the pharmacologic properties 228 alone are not sufficient evidence of effectiveness and safety). Although a sponsor cannot rely on 229 information from other stimulant drug products for the evidence of effectiveness and safety, 230 knowledge of the class and the indication can help to inform the drug development program. 231
candidates.context: IV. NEW MOLECULAR ENTITY 225 • A demonstration of safety and effectiveness of stimulant drugs for the treatment of 233 ADHD in 4- to 5-year-old pediatric patients would require at least one adequate and well- 234 controlled clinical study in this population (21 CFR 314.126); this study should be a 235 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study. A placebo control is 236 necessary to provide interpretable results. The timing of such a study would depend 237 largely on what is known about the safety of the particular investigational drug. FDA 238 encourages sponsors to discuss the details and timing of the 4- to 5-year-old pediatric 239 patient portion of the drug development programs early, preferably before initiating 240 studies in 6- to 12-year-old pediatric patients. 241
